function.name: select
function.arguments:
{"query":"SELECT
  url,
  title,
  published_at,
  SEM_EXTRACT_ALL(
    content,
    'a named public-facing World Wide Web search engine, metasearch engine, search portal, or answer/search engine; include both active and defunct services, but exclude site-specific internal search tools, enterprise-only software, and database search interfaces',
    engine := 'search engine or service name',
    launch_year := 'year first launched publicly, YYYY; NULL if unstated',
    end_year := 'year discontinued or shut down, YYYY; NULL if active or unstated',
    status := 'current operating status stated by the page',
    country_or_region := 'country or principal market stated by the page',
    type := 'type or specialization stated by the page',
    evidence := 'per_field'
  ) AS engines
FROM WEB_SEARCH(
  'comprehensive list web search engines active defunct historical',
  'timeline web search engines history Archie W3Catalog Aliweb JumpStation',
  'list of search engines privacy metasearch regional 2026',
  'defunct search engines list AltaVista Lycos Excite HotBot',
  'modern AI search engines list ChatGPT Search Perplexity You.com Brave Kagi',
  'international search engines Baidu Yandex Naver Seznam Sogou list',
  'independent search engines own index Mojeek Brave Yep Marginalia Stract',
  'site:en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_search_engines',
  'site:searchenginemap.com search engines map',
  'historical internet search engines directory 1990s 2000s'
)
WHERE SEM_MATCH(content, 'contains a list, directory, comparison, or historical timeline naming multiple World Wide Web search engines')","show_preview":true}

function.arguments:
{"query":"WITH candidates AS (
  SELECT
    engine,
    launch_year,
    end_year,
    status,
    region,
    category,
    url,
    title,
    'reference' AS source_group,
    5 AS source_weight
  FROM r4b419d08b13

  UNION ALL

  SELECT
    engine,
    launch_year,
    NULL AS end_year,
    status,
    region,
    category,
    url,
    title,
    'modern/general' AS source_group,
    3 AS source_weight
  FROM rae8656c6963

  UNION ALL

  SELECT
    engine,
    launch_year,
    end_year,
    status,
    region,
    category,
    url,
    title,
    'regional' AS source_group,
    3 AS source_weight
  FROM rff325229ad0

  UNION ALL

  SELECT
    engine,
    launch_year,
    end_year,
    status,
    region,
    category,
    url,
    title,
    'specialized' AS source_group,
    3 AS source_weight
  FROM r820f5feacbe

  UNION ALL

  SELECT
    engine,
    launch_year,
    NULL AS end_year,
    status,
    region,
    category,
    url,
    title,
    'AI search' AS source_group,
    4 AS source_weight
  FROM rd6f5e01763c
),
clean AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT
    engine,
    launch_year,
    end_year,
    status,
    region,
    category,
    url,
    title,
    source_group,
    source_weight
  FROM candidates
  WHERE engine IS NOT NULL
    AND length(trim(engine)) BETWEEN 2 AND 100
    AND lower(trim(engine)) NOT IN (
      'search engine',
      'search engines',
      'web search',
      'ai search',
      'internet',
      'world wide web',
      'comparison of search engines',
      'list of search engines'
    )
),
rolled AS (
  SELECT
    SEM_NORM(engine, 'merge spelling, capitalization, punctuation, and former-versus-current branding only when unmistakably the same public search service; keep distinct products and search modes separate') AS engine,
    MIN(TRY_CAST(launch_year AS INTEGER)) AS launch_year,
    MAX(TRY_CAST(end_year AS INTEGER)) AS end_year,
    MODE(status) FILTER (WHERE status IS NOT NULL AND trim(status) <> '') AS reported_status,
    MODE(region) FILTER (WHERE region IS NOT NULL AND trim(region) <> '') AS region,
    string_agg(
      DISTINCT COALESCE(
        NULLIF(trim(category), ''),
        CASE source_group
          WHEN 'AI search' THEN 'AI search / answer engine'
          WHEN 'regional' THEN 'regional search'
          WHEN 'specialized' THEN 'specialized search'
          WHEN 'modern/general' THEN 'modern web search'
          ELSE 'web search / directory / metasearch'
        END
      ),
      '; '
      ORDER BY COALESCE(
        NULLIF(trim(category), ''),
        CASE source_group
          WHEN 'AI search' THEN 'AI search / answer engine'
          WHEN 'regional' THEN 'regional search'
          WHEN 'specialized' THEN 'specialized search'
          WHEN 'modern/general' THEN 'modern web search'
          ELSE 'web search / directory / metasearch'
        END
      )
    ) AS categories,
    COUNT(DISTINCT url) AS source_count,
    ARG_MAX(url, source_weight) AS source_url,
    ARG_MAX(title, source_weight) AS source_title,
    BOOL_OR(source_group = 'reference') AS in_reference_lists,
    BOOL_OR(source_group = 'AI search') AS modern_ai_candidate
  FROM clean
  GROUP BY SEM_NORM(engine, 'merge spelling, capitalization, punctuation, and former-versus-current branding only when unmistakably the same public search service; keep distinct products and search modes separate')
)
SELECT
  engine,
  launch_year,
  end_year,
  CASE
    WHEN end_year IS NOT NULL THEN COALESCE(reported_status, 'defunct/discontinued')
    ELSE reported_status
  END AS reported_status,
  region,
  categories,
  source_count,
  source_title,
  source_url
FROM rolled
WHERE in_reference_lists
   OR source_count >= 3
   OR (modern_ai_candidate AND source_count >= 2)
ORDER BY
  launch_year NULLS LAST,
  engine","show_preview":false}

{"brief":"The user asked verbatim: “List all search engines existed in history. Make sure not to miss any modern ones.” Treat “all” as an open-ended historical catalogue rather than a provably complete universe: no authoritative registry exists, names and brands change, regional and short-lived engines are poorly archived, and the boundary between web search, directories, portals, vertical search, metasearch, and AI answer engines is fuzzy. State this limitation prominently and do not claim literal completeness.

The research scanned broad historical timelines and lists plus modern, regional, specialized, privacy, decentralized, and 2023–2026 AI-search sources. After normalization and evidence thresholds, it produced 1,253 catalogued public-facing search-service names. Of these, 390 have a sourced launch year, from 1982 through 2026; 100 are explicitly ended/inactive by available fields; and 258 are classified somewhere in the source evidence as AI search or answer-engine names. Many statuses and dates remain blank rather than guessed. The modern search specifically included 2026 material, current as of 2026-08-31.

r53de7ff9f34 is the full catalogue, one row per normalized service name, ordered by launch year then name. It has launch/end year when sourced, reported status, region, category labels, number of independent source URLs mentioning the name, and a clickable best source. Make this searchable/filterable and downloadable. Lead with one bold visual timeline or era view, but keep the complete table central because the user explicitly requested a list. Allow filters for launch era, status, categories (especially AI search / answer engines), and region. Do not infer “active” from a blank end year; display blank as unresolved.

r1f191a7c1c8 contains precomputed totals and era counts. Use it for KPI cards and an era chart; do not calculate counts yourself. Emphasize the explosion of modern AI-search names in the 2020s and the large unresolved-date pool, which reflects incomplete historical documentation and permissive inclusion rather than a clean census.

Visual style: beautiful archival-to-futuristic “history of search” design, excellent typography and readability, a chronological hero visual, compact KPI cards, and a highly usable catalogue. Clearly distinguish sourced fact, reported classification, and missing data. Add a methodology/definition note: included public-facing WWW search engines, metasearch services, search portals, notable vertical/specialized engines, decentralized/privacy engines, and named AI answer/search products; excluded site-internal search boxes, browser find, desktop-only local file search, enterprise-only software, and API-only products without a public search experience. I compiled a searchable historical catalogue of **1,253 search-service names**, covering early systems through modern AI search engines as of **August 31, 2026**.

No catalogue can guarantee literal completeness—there is no universal registry, and many regional or short-lived engines were poorly archived—but the report includes historical, regional, specialized, privacy, decentralized, metasearch, and AI-answer services.
